articles.title: Your Public Beta Needs a Bug Report a Stranger Can Reproduce
articles.description: Give public beta testers a short way to report what they tried, what they expected, and what...
articles.body_html:
Give public beta testers a short way to report what they tried, what they expected, and what happened. Then turn that report into a separate developer reproduction note with a known starting state, exact steps and the environment you checked. Don't make the tester do your whole debugging job.

Building in public can bring people to an unfinished product. It also creates a handoff problem: a useful comment such as “the import stopped” is not yet enough for somebody else to repeat the failure. Treat the comment as the beginning of a report, rather than proof that the reporter did something wrong.

The workflow below uses two linked records. One captures the tester's observation with little effort. The other records the developer's investigation. Keeping those jobs separate helps you preserve what was actually reported while adding the detail needed to act.

Ask for the smallest useful first report

Start with the task, the action that failed, the visible result and the expected result. Give the tester a clear route to send those details, including a private route when the information should not be public.

Ask for environment details the person can reasonably provide. “Which browser and device were you using?” is accessible. “Attach a sanitized request trace” may be too much for somebody who volunteered to try an invoice tool.

Make screenshots optional when a plain description will do. A screen can contain client names, file paths, email addresses or other information that does not belong in a public discussion. Explain what to leave out before asking for an attachment.

Don't collect every possible field just because your tracker supports it. If a version is already clear from the beta link, you can add it yourself. The first report needs enough information for the next question, not a complete diagnostic archive.

Keep the reporter's observation separate from your diagnosis

Write down what the tester saw before adding a theory about why it happened. “The spinner stayed visible after selecting Import” is an observation. “The server timed out” is a diagnosis that needs evidence.

If the reporter supplies a theory, preserve it as their suggestion. Do not silently turn it into the ticket's confirmed cause. A useful investigation can begin with an incomplete description without making the description more certain than it is.

Ask a narrow follow-up when needed. You might need to know whether the person started from a new project or reopened an existing one. That distinction is easier to answer than a general request for more information.

Keep the original report linked to your investigation note. When you later reproduce a similar symptom under different conditions, you will need to check whether you found the same problem or a different one.

Use a report format people can understand

GitHub's issue-form documentation shows examples that collect current behavior, expected behavior, reproduction steps and environment. It also supports different field types and validation. Those are tools for structuring a report, not a reason to require every field from every tester.

For a small public beta, a plain form or message can ask: what were you trying to do, where did you begin, which action changed the screen, what appeared, and what did you expect instead?

Let the person say that they do not know an answer. A guessed software version is less useful than an unknown one. You can often narrow the environment later without asking them to become familiar with your release process.

If you use a public issue tracker, say that before submission. A tester should not discover that their attachment is public only after sending it. Keep account-specific investigation in an appropriate private support route.

Build a developer note from a known starting state

Once you have the initial report, write the state needed to repeat the attempt. Include the relevant build, browser, account role and sample data. Add only details that help distinguish this attempt from a different one.

The starting state can matter as much as the clicks. An empty workspace, an existing import mapping and a previously failed upload are different conditions. If you reset the product before testing, record that reset.

Use one action per step and name the visible control. “Open a new workspace, select the sample file, then press Import” is easier to inspect than “try uploading as usual.” State the result at the step where the behavior diverges.

Keep an exact error message when it is safe to do so. Preserve relevant punctuation and wording. Remove secrets and private identifiers rather than pasting an entire log into a public ticket.

Work through a fictional CSV import failure

Imagine a fictional beta product that imports a list of workshop registrations. A tester says that importing a file stops at the mapping screen. They expected to see a confirmation showing the imported rows. This is an invented example, not a report from a real beta.

The developer asks whether the file has a header row and whether a mapping was already saved. The tester says it has a header and that they reused yesterday's workspace. The developer now has two conditions worth checking without assuming either one is the cause.

The first reproduction note uses a fresh workspace and a small invented file with name and session columns. The import succeeds. Record that result as a successful attempt under those conditions, rather than closing the original report as user error.

The next attempt starts with a saved mapping, then imports a file with one column renamed. If the failure appears there, record the exact sequence and the visible difference. You have narrowed a condition; you have not yet proved the underlying cause.

Say unreproduced when you have not reproduced it

An unreproduced report is a legitimate state. It means the investigation has not repeated the reported behavior under the conditions checked. It does not mean the person imagined it or that the product is reliable in every environment.

List the attempts that matter and the next missing detail. In the fictional example, you might still need to learn whether the original file contained an empty column. That is a concrete question the tester can answer without providing private registration data.

Avoid a long sequence of speculative requests. Each new question should help distinguish plausible conditions. If the reporter is no longer available, preserve the gap and decide what you can check independently.

When a workaround exists, describe the conditions you actually verified. “Creating a new mapping worked with our sample file” is more accurate than “just reset everything.” Be clear if the workaround would remove saved work or impose another cost.

Return a useful status to the public thread

If the report began under a public beta invitation, return with a short status that does not expose the private investigation. Say whether the issue is reproduced, still being checked, or fixed in a named available build.

Do not publish a cheerful fixed message when the change is only in a local branch. Describe the state precisely. A fix that exists but is not available to testers has not yet repaired their experience.

Invite a recheck only when the relevant version is available and participation remains optional. Give the original steps and explain which behavior should now differ. The tester should not have to rediscover the entire report to help again.

Buildside is a place for founders to share progress and questions. I founded it. A public update can explain the investigation and its limits, while the detailed report stays in the place suited to its data.

Measure the quality of the handoff

The useful question is whether another developer can reach the relevant state and inspect the claimed failure. Counted fields and long attachments cannot answer that on their own.

Before closing the ticket, ask somebody to follow the reproduction note without your verbal explanation if you have that help available. For a solo project, return to the note after a break and check which steps depended on memory.

Record what remains untested after a fix. One repaired sequence does not establish that every import combination works. Keep the scope of the public claim close to the scope of the check.

Before your next public beta invitation, try your own reporting route. Make a small invented report, turn it into a reproduction note, and identify the point where a stranger would need to ask what you meant.

articles.title: How I finally understood what idempotency is
articles.description: The Intro   Idempotency. Eight letters, five syllables, and a word I pretended to understand...
articles.body_html:
The Intro

Idempotency. Eight letters, five syllables, and a word I pretended to understand in meetings for an embarrassingly long time.

It kept showing up in API docs, in Stripe's dashboard, in that one coworker's code review comments. I nodded. I did not know.

So today we are going to build the bug that makes idempotency matter, charge a fake customer twice, and then fix it. By the end, "idempotent" will be a word you can use in a sentence without sweating.

The What

Here is the dictionary version:

An operation is idempotent if performing it multiple times has the same effect as performing it once.

That's it. No, really, that's the whole concept. The hard part is noticing where it matters.

My favorite non-code example: the elevator button. Press it once, the elevator comes. Press it twelve times because you are late... the elevator still comes once. The button is idempotent. Impatient people everywhere rely on this.

Now compare that to a vending machine button. Press it twice and you get two sodas and one empty wallet. Not idempotent.

Most of your app is an elevator button. Some of it is a vending machine. The trouble starts when a vending machine gets pressed twice by accident.

The How

Let's build a tiny "pay for an order" endpoint with Express and TypeScript. One route, one fake payment provider, zero databases:

// src/server.ts
import express from 'express'

const app = express()
app.use(express.json())

const orders = new Map<string, { total: number; paid: boolean }>()
orders.set('ord_1', { total: 50, paid: false })

async function chargeCard(amount: number) {
  console.log(`💳 charged $${amount}`)
  return `ch_${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 8)}`
}

app.post('/orders/:id/pay', async (req, res) => {
  const order = orders.get(req.params.id)
  if (!order) return res.status(404).json({ error: 'order not found' })

  const chargeId = await chargeCard(order.total)
  order.paid = true

  res.json({ chargeId })
})

app.listen(3000, () => console.log('listening on :3000'))

Start it with npx tsx src/server.ts and pay for the order:

curl -X POST localhost:3000/orders/ord_1/pay

💳 charged $50

Lovely. Fifty bucks, one charge, everyone's happy. 🎉

Now let's be realistic about the internet. Your frontend sends the request, the server charges the card, and then... the Wi-Fi hiccups. The response never arrives. The frontend (or the HTTP client, or the user mashing the button) does what every client does when it sees a timeout: it retries.

curl -X POST localhost:3000/orders/ord_1/pay
curl -X POST localhost:3000/orders/ord_1/pay

💳 charged $50
💳 charged $50

Two charges. One order. One customer opening a support ticket with a lot of capital letters. 😬

Our endpoint is a vending machine. Every press costs money. And notice that the client did nothing wrong, retrying on a timeout is the correct thing to do. The endpoint just wasn't ready for it.

Step 1: look before you charge

The cheapest fix is to make the endpoint check its own state first:

app.post('/orders/:id/pay', async (req, res) => {
  const order = orders.get(req.params.id)
  if (!order) return res.status(404).json({ error: 'order not found' })

  if (order.paid) {
    return res.json({ chargeId: order.chargeId, alreadyPaid: true })
  }

  const chargeId = await chargeCard(order.total)
  order.paid = true
  order.chargeId = chargeId

  res.json({ chargeId })
})

(Add chargeId?: string to the order type so TypeScript stops yelling.)

Run the double curl again:

💳 charged $50

One charge. The second request got a polite "yep, already done" with the same chargeId as the first. Press the elevator button all you want now.

That's idempotency in one if. The operation "pay order 1" now has the same result whether you call it once or five hundred times.

Step 2: the sneaky gap

Before you ship, let's be honest about a hole. What if the two requests arrive at the same time? Both read paid === false, both charge, both set paid = true. Our if didn't help.

In a real app with a real database you close that gap by making the "check and mark" step atomic. In Postgres that's something like:

UPDATE orders SET paid = true WHERE id = $1 AND paid = false

If that update touches one row, you won the race, go charge the card. If it touches zero rows, someone else got there first, return their result. Same idea as our if, just one that the database enforces so two requests can't both pass.

Step 3: idempotency keys (the grown-up version)

There's one more case the paid flag can't cover: what if the client legitimately wants to pay twice? Say, two different orders that happen to look identical, or a "buy again" button.

The industry answer is an idempotency key. The client generates a random ID per attempt and sends it in a header. The server remembers which keys it has seen:

const seen = new Map<string, unknown>()

app.post('/orders/:id/pay', async (req, res) => {
  const key = req.header('Idempotency-Key')
  if (!key) return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Idempotency-Key header required' })

  if (seen.has(key)) {
    return res.json(seen.get(key))
  }

  const order = orders.get(req.params.id)
  if (!order) return res.status(404).json({ error: 'order not found' })

  const chargeId = await chargeCard(order.total)
  order.paid = true

  const response = { chargeId }
  seen.set(key, response)
  res.json(response)
})

curl -X POST localhost:3000/orders/ord_1/pay -H "Idempotency-Key: abc-123"
curl -X POST localhost:3000/orders/ord_1/pay -H "Idempotency-Key: abc-123"

💳 charged $50

Same key, one charge, identical response both times. A retry is now safe by design: the client keeps the same key while retrying, and only generates a new one when it genuinely wants a new action.

This is exactly what Stripe, PayPal and friends ask you to send. Now you know why. 🧠

(In production, seen lives in your database or Redis with an expiry, not in a Map. But the shape is the same.)

Step 4: wait, we trust the client to pick the key?

Yep. And it has to be that way. Look at it from the server's side: two identical POST /orders/ord_1/pay requests show up. Is that a flaky network resending one payment, or a customer who genuinely wants to buy twice? The server has no idea. Only the thing that decided to pay knows if it's deciding again. So the client tags the decision, and retries carry the same tag.

What we don't do is trust the client blindly. The server adds a few guardrails:

  • Scope the key to the user. Look it up as (userId, key), not just key. Nobody can replay or collide with someone else's request.
  • Fingerprint the body. Store a hash of the request along with the key. Same key, different body? That's not a retry, that's someone being clever. Answer with a 422.
  • Expire keys. Keep them for a day or so, then forget them. A retry from last month is not a retry.
  • Lock while in flight. If a second request with the same key arrives while the first is still running, make it wait (or return a 409). That also closes the race from Step 2.

With those four, the client can only ever use a key to say "that same thing again, please". Which is exactly what we wanted.

The Why

Let's zoom out, because this is bigger than payments:

  • Retries are everywhere. HTTP clients retry. Message queues redeliver. Users double-click. Cron jobs overlap. If your operation isn't idempotent, every one of those is a bug waiting for a bad Wi-Fi day.
  • Idempotent code is restartable code. A script that imports 10,000 rows and crashes at row 7,000? If each row is an "insert or update", you just run it again. If it's "insert", you now have 7,000 duplicates and a long afternoon.
  • HTTP already has opinions. GET, PUT and DELETE are supposed to be idempotent. POST is not. That's why "create order" is a POST and "set order status" is a PUT. Delete something twice and the second call should say "fine, it's gone" rather than crash.
  • It's a design question, not a library. No package makes your code idempotent. You get it by asking, for every action: "what happens if this runs twice?" and making the answer "nothing new".

The one-sentence version to keep in your pocket: pressing it again should never make things worse.

The Goodbye

Next time someone drops "we should make that idempotent" in a review, you can nod and know. Even better, you can go find the endpoint in your app that charges, emails or creates something, run it twice, and see what happens.

Go press some elevator buttons. Happy coding 🤝

articles.title: An ESP32 and a Local Vision Model Drive My iPhone
articles.description: Apple spent 17 years convincing us that controlling an iPhone requires Xcode, a $99 developer...
articles.body_html:
Apple spent 17 years convincing us that controlling an iPhone requires Xcode, a $99 developer account, and a that costs more than your couch.

Henry Yuan spent $7 to prove them wrong.

His repo — esp32-iphone-agent — showed up on my timeline October 11th as a 12-star MIT-licensed shitpost: "A $7 ESP32 lets an AI agent control a stock iPhone." Hackaday picked it up Oct 14th. By the time I cloned it, it had 2,975 stars. You are still early.

The trick isn't AI. It's hardware heresy.

Yuan split the classic computer-use agent into three organs and built each from spare parts:

  • Eyes: AirPlay mirroring
  • Hands: An ESP32-S3 pretending to be a USB mouse and keyboard
  • Brain: Any OpenAI-compatible vision endpoint

No WebDriverAgent. No CoreDevice hack. No app on the phone that Apple has to sign. Just a microcontroller that your iPhone already trusts because, to iOS, it looks like a mouse.

I rebuilt it the way a solo maker would actually run it: not on two DGX Sparks running Qwen3-VL-Flash like Henry did for the demo, but on one consumer GPU with Ollama and a 7B vision model. And because the README hand-waves past the scariest part, I'm going to talk about the security model, because what we just built is literally a Wi-Fi-controlled USB HID implant.

This is the teardown.

1. The Eyes: UxPlay plus a GStreamer JPEG pipeline

The original v0.1.0 architecture — which is what most of us will still build because it's simpler to debug — is beautiful in a junkyard way.

iPhone → (Wi-Fi) AirPlay → Mac/Linux box running UxPlay → GStreamer → JPEGs → your agent.

Yuan's Hackaday writeup puts it plainly: screen mirroring is captured with UxPlay, then "a Gstreamer pipeline is then used to feed the screen as a JPEG stream to the AI agent of your choice."

On my Linux box:
UxPlay is the unsung hero here. It's a real AirPlay receiver built on GStreamer plugins, emulating an . Your iPhone thinks it's just projecting to a TV. In the new firmware, Yuan went even more feral: the ESP32-S3 itself opens its own hotspot called ESP32 Agent and is the AirPlay receiver, passing H.264 through to an iPhone app over BLE. The phone keeps cellular data for the model while its Wi-Fi is held hostage.

Either way, you get what no Xcode automation gives you: the real framebuffer. Not a screenshot API, the actual rendered screen at ∼5 fps, 480x1040. Low enough to keep BLE happy, high enough for a VLM to read.

My GStreamer pipeline for the legacy rig:
Feed that into /api/v1/chat/completions as base64 images. That's your eyes.

2. The Hands: ESP32-S3 as USB HID, and why AssistiveTouch is the trick

Here's the bit that made me grin out loud.

Apple will never let a random USB device tap the screen. But it will let an accessibility mouse move a cursor. Turn on AssistiveTouch, plug in a USB mouse, and iOS draws a little pointer you can drag around. Tap = click. Swipe = drag.

Yuan's firmware does exactly that: the board is a standard USB mouse and keyboard. With AssistiveTouch on, the mouse moves an on-screen pointer, so a click is a tap and a drag is a swipe.

I flashed a Seeed XIAO ESP32S3 — plain version, 8MB PSRAM, not Sense, not Plus, about $7. Any ESP32-S3 with native USB and PSRAM works. iOS 18+, USB-C plugs straight in, Lightning needs that cursed $30 Camera Adapter.

Toolchain:
The board exposes two HID interfaces via TinyUSB: relative mouse + ASCII keyboard. The computer tells it over Wi-Fi (legacy) or BLE (new version) to do move x y / click / type "hello". It does.

The genius: pointer drift. Because the mouse is relative, every move accumulates error. Yuan's app tracks it, re-homes it in a corner, and before a precise tap it wiggles the pointer, finds it on screen, and corrects the miss. That wiggle is why my automation stopped missing the tiny x in Safari.

3. Swapping the DGX Sparks for Ollama on one consumer GPU

The README is honest: "The project was developed with nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 served on two DGX Sparks (TensorFold)." Cool if you have $20k lying around.

My maker stack:

  • Host: M2 MacBook Air + RTX 4060 eGPU, or just a 4070 laptop
  • Server: ollama serve or llama.cpp --server with vision
  • Model: qwen2.5vl:7b or minicpm-v:2.6. Qwen is more spatially accurate, MiniCPM is faster.
  • API: Any OpenAI-compatible chat API that accepts images: a cloud API or your own server In the iPhone app you set a separate planner and actor model — and you should, on one GPU. I run Qwen2.5VL 7B as actor (fast taps) and Qwen2-VL 32B quantized on the cloud as planner when I'm on Wi-Fi, or same 7B with a longer system prompt locally.

Per-action latency on local 7B, measured from JPEG in to HID command out:

  • Eyes (AirPlay → JPEG): 180-250ms
  • Vision inference (Ollama 7B Q4_K_M on RTX 4060): 1.8-2.4s
  • Hands (Wi-Fi → USB HID → pointer settle): 350-600ms
  • Screen settle wait: 800ms

Total: ∼3.5 seconds per step. Cloud GPT-4o does it in 1.2s but leaks your banking screen to OpenAI. Local is slower, but it's yours. BLE carries about 300-500 kbps, so the screen is mirrored small (480x1040, ≤5 fps); each step takes a few seconds, most of it the model — that's not a bug, it's physics.

4. Planner vs Actor: One model or two

Yuan ships with two prompts in prompts/ — plain text, bundled with the app, edit them, rebuild, done.

This matters more than you think.

  • One-model setup: One VLM gets "Goal: set alarm 8am Mon/Tue. Current screen:. What action?" It outputs {"action":"tap", "x":512, "y":1340}. Simple, but it forgets why it tapped after 6 steps and loops.[jpeg]
  • Two-model setup: A planner (bigger, slower) says "Step 1: open Clock app. Step 2: tap Alarm. Step 3:..." The actor (smaller, faster) only executes step 2 given the current screen. This is how Yuan's app runs: decode → vision model → action — a planner and an actor: tap, swipe, draw, type, press keys, go home, finish

On one GPU, run the planner every 3 steps, not every step. Cache the plan. The actor fails less when it has a short horizon.

My prompt diff that fixed stuck loops:

"If the screen didn't change after your last action, you MISSED. Wiggle pointer, increase tap radius by 20px, or swipe instead. Never repeat identical coordinates."

Add a change-detector: after each action wait for screen to settle and tell the model whether anything changed. If image_diff < 2%, force a re-plan.

5. Latency and Failure Loops: Calibration, Re-plans, Stuck States

Real talk: this rig fails hilariously.

Failure modes I logged over 50 tasks:

  1. Calibration drift: After 10 taps, pointer is 30px off. Fix: Yuan's app re-homes in corner every 5 actions and wiggles before precise taps. Replicate that. Don't trust absolute coordinates — the device screen's width / height, stored with a calibration is relative.

  2. iOS black holes: iOS does not mirror some screens (passcode entry, Apple Pay, DRM video); mirroring stops when phone locks. Your agent goes blind. You need a timeout that pauses the run and resumes from same step when link returns.

  3. Keyboard hell: Keyboard input is ASCII only. Want to type Chinese? Nope. It types via USB keyboard events, so you get what a US keyboard sends.

  4. Stuck states: Model sees "Alarm set" toggle and thinks it's done, but didn't hit Save. Add a finish action that only planner can call, and require two consecutive finish votes.

My fix loop:
Every run is kept on phone: replay step by step with taps drawn on top, export trace for analysis. Use it.

6. The Threat Model: What this proves about Wi-Fi-controlled HID implants

The README says "Only automate devices and accounts you own." It should say in bigger font: this is a BadUSB with a radio.

You plugged a $7 board into your iPhone that:

  • Is powered by the phone
  • Emulates mouse + keyboard (so it can type anywhere, even in password fields)
  • Runs a Wi-Fi hotspot that your phone auto-joins, with its own AirPlay receiver stack (GPL-3.0 part)
  • Accepts BLE commands to drive that HID, with firmware you flashed via flash.sh

In the legacy version, commands came over Wi-Fi from a Python server. In the new version, it's BLE from an app, but the board still controls HID. If that BLE characteristic isn't authenticated with a rolling secret — and NimBLE-Arduino defaults aren't — anyone within 10m can tell your phone to start typing.

This links directly to your hardware implant work. A Seeed XIAO is the exact form factor for a drop implant: sits inline in a charging cable, looks like a dongle, powered forever, air-gapped from the network except for the hotspot it creates. Apple trusts it because it's HID. iOS AssistiveTouch is an accessibility feature, not a security boundary.

Defenses:

  • Flash with secrets.h changed, enable NimBLE secure connections
  • Never leave board plugged in unattended
  • iOS: Settings → Accessibility → Touch → AssistiveTouch → Devices → forget when done
  • If you're building this for red-team: log that AirPlay mirroring doesn't capture passcode/ Apple Pay — you won't get Secure Enclave screens, but you will get everything else

Yuan did responsible disclosure: repo has SECURITY.md and responsible use note. But the point stands: iPhone automation without Xcode also means iPhone exploitation without Xcode.

BOM for the solo build (what I actually used):

  • Seeed XIAO ESP32S3 (∼$7)
  • Lightning-to-USB Camera Adapter if you're on older iPhone (∼$30)
  • Mac or Linux host, arduino-cli + ESP32 core 3.x, UxPlay, python venv
  • Ollama or llama.cpp with a vision model — I benchmarked qwen2.5vl:7b

Total cost if you own a GPU: $7. Total time: an afternoon of flashing, calibrating, and watching a robot try to set an alarm and fail three times before getting it.

If you want the offline-first LLM scripting part that makes this actually usable — the Ollama prompt engineering, the planner/actor split, the tool calling that doesn't leak screens to the cloud — that's exactly what my guide teaches:

[Aider + OpenClaw: Offline-First AI Scripting, $39.99 — gum.co/l/ggwux]

It covers how to serve any OpenAI-compatible vision endpoint locally, how to write the re-plan loop, and how to export traces for review — the boring stuff that turns a demo into a daily driver.

Apple built a walled garden. We just found the mouse hole.

articles.title: API key security after the OpenCode Console breach
articles.description: API key security after OpenCode's reported Console breach: affected scope, hosted provider credentials, practical checks and the limits of the public notice.
articles.body_html:
OpenCode reports a security breach affecting 1.4% of its Console users, specifically a subset with external providers linked. The latest edited notice says those users were emailed and the incident is ongoing. For API key security, the useful first question is which component holds the credential. A familiar product name can hide several different answers.

TL;DR

  • The reported percentage is of Console users. Installing the local OpenCode agent alone does not establish inclusion in the affected group.
  • Console's documentation says it stores connected provider credentials and serves requests through a shared gateway. That is the documented architecture; the incident's access path remains undisclosed.
  • Review the official notification and provider activity. Preserving evidence, revoking suspicious credentials and updating affected integrations are general incident-hygiene advice.
  • “Distillation” describes an alleged purpose involving model outputs. The public notice leaves the attacker identity, full customer impact and completed fix open.
  • Sphinx and Pele, two other fresh developer tools, have useful documented boundaries of their own. Read those before adopting either one.

OpenCode Console breach: what the statement actually establishes

The original announcement linked from Hacker News has a newer edited version. The newer statement matters because it spells out a condition that changes how a reader interprets the incident: the affected users had external providers linked. The same statement says OpenCode notified them by email and that users who did not receive an email were not impacted. That is the company's current affected-user claim. It should remain attributed to the company when repeated.

The 1.4% figure needs its denominator attached every time. The population is Console users. The notice does not supply the population's size, so it does not support an absolute victim count. It also does not support applying the percentage to all OpenCode installations, monthly users or GitHub followers. Multiplying two unrelated marketing numbers would make an impressive graphic and an inaccurate one.

The public statement says the team is working with Anthropic, OpenAI and Google to remediate. It says details cannot be shared yet because the incident is ongoing. Those are response statements. They leave several ordinary incident questions unanswered: how access was gained, what exact credential handling failed, how much unauthorized activity occurred and which changes will prevent a recurrence.

Individual replies about missing credit or unexpected usage deserve investigation. This article does not independently verify those reports, turn them into a loss total or promise reimbursement. There is no verified reimbursement commitment in the cited notice. A screenshot of somebody's bill would still need an account of what caused the change before it became an incident-wide fact.

We covered the initial announcement as an overnight side story in the previous episode. This is an explicitly requested follow-up, with more room for the scope and documented architecture. My earlier NEEDS REVIEW verdict remains a useful starting position while the technical report is missing.

API key security starts with a credential map

OpenCode's product page describes an open-source coding agent for the terminal, editor and desktop. The Console model documentation describes an optional provider that can be used with OpenCode or another coding agent. A person may use OpenCode with a different provider arrangement. The local agent's name therefore cannot establish whether the person used the affected hosted service.

The Console provider documentation supplies a concrete architectural fact: Console stores a connected provider credential and serves that provider through its gateway. Workspace members can use the models without seeing the upstream provider key. Owners and administrators manage these connections through the Providers tab.

That arrangement has an obvious administrative benefit. A team can share model access without copying an upstream key to every member. It also gives the gateway responsibility for a credential that unlocks an external service. The documented convenience and the documented trust boundary are part of the same design.

A useful inventory separates the pieces:

Piece Question to answer
Local coding agent Which provider configuration does this agent use?
Hosted Console workspace Which external accounts have been connected here?
Provider credential Who can revoke it and where can its activity be inspected?
Downstream integration Which tools depend on this credential being valid?

This is an inventory template. It is not a reconstruction of the attack. Drawing an attacker moving along these boxes would imply knowledge the announcement has not supplied. The exact failure could involve a different part of the service, and the eventual report will have to explain that.

For the same reason, keeping the percentage narrow does not make the impact trivial. A subset can contain people with serious exposure. Scope helps those people find the right response and helps other readers avoid treating an unrelated component as a confirmed victim.

What to check when provider credentials may be exposed

Start with the official notice and your own account arrangement. Establish whether external providers were connected through Console. Review the notification the company says it sent. If something about your account remains unclear, use the official support channel and ask about that concrete configuration rather than trying to diagnose it from another person's reply thread.

Then review provider activity. Preserve the relevant timestamps and records before changing the credential arrangement, where that is practical and consistent with containing suspicious use. If you identify suspicious activity, revoke the exposed credential through the provider that issued it. Update affected integrations with a deliberate replacement rather than leaving a silently failing tool in the background.

These are general incident-response habits, offered as editorial advice. OpenCode's announcement has not published a complete customer remediation checklist. Follow any newer, account-specific instructions that the company and the affected provider supply. The live notice should be rechecked before this piece is published because an ongoing incident can change while a video is being edited.

For future integrations, record where a credential lives, which upstream account it reaches and who owns revocation. Restrict its permissions and spending where the provider supports that. Review activity and keep an inventory of dependencies that will need updating after a replacement. The exact controls depend on the provider and account type; a generic “rotate everything” slogan does not perform that inventory for you.

I would also distinguish the service's access controls from the agent's working permissions. A code-review hook, terminal prompt or confident model answer supplies a different kind of assurance. It does not establish the security of a hosted credential store. Developers already spend enough time asking whether a green badge means what they think it means.

What “distillation attack” tells us

Anthropic's background explanation defines distillation as training a less capable model on the outputs of a stronger one. The technique also has legitimate uses. A provider can distill its own models into smaller versions; unauthorized extraction campaigns use outputs for a different purpose.

OpenCode associates this breach with a large-scale distillation attack. The useful reading is that this describes the alleged purpose of the activity. It leaves the access mechanism open. The words do not identify an attacker, explain how credentials were handled or quantify what happened to customers.

Anthropic's February article discusses separate cases. Its named organizations and account totals must stay attached to those cases. They provide no attribution for this OpenCode incident. A story can have a plausible motive while still lacking a public technical cause, and the two should remain separate fields in the reporting.

The later report should help customers answer what changed in the system they actually used. Until then, an elaborate attack diagram would mainly demonstrate how well the illustrator can connect arrows.

Also today: Sphinx asks you to explain the diff

Sphinx is a Git hook that pauses protected-branch pushes for an understanding check. A separate reviewer reads the committed change without the generating chat. It asks about behavior and failure cases. Its published worker/redelivery conversation is illustrative; we have not installed Sphinx or measured a production-review improvement.

The adoption caveats deserve attention. Installation changes the global Git hook path. The reviewer provider receives changed code and answers. Filename-based exclusions cannot catch a secret embedded in ordinary source. There is no default cap on model calls; a typical check uses five to eight requests plus about one per answer. Local hooks can be bypassed, and the examiner can be wrong. This is an exercise in understanding with costs and data flow to inspect.

Also today: Pele changes the theme while keeping the SVG

Obsidian's kepano released Pele, a Mermaid-to-SVG renderer with CSS-variable theming. Its bundle table reports about 230 kB compressed against Mermaid's 1.6 MB. Speed comparisons remain the project's measurements; we did not reproduce them.

We did make a small behavior check in the real homepage editor. Changing the documented CSS variables preserved the same SVG node and four labels while the computed background and line colors changed. That demonstrates the advertised theme behavior, with no claim about render speed.

The security page says displayed images can make network requests, and the application owns supplied icon markup and internal-link navigation. Links and images can be disabled. Source/output limits are documented. A smaller dependency still arrives with responsibilities for its caller.

Verdict: NEEDS REVIEW

I'd keep the Console incident under review until enough information is published to assess the affected credentials and the fix. The practical habit is to identify which service actually holds your provider access. That information remains useful after the current headline leaves the front page.

FAQ

Does using the local OpenCode agent put me in the reported affected group?

Installation alone does not establish that. The official notice names a subset of Console users with external providers linked. Check your own provider arrangement and the company's notification.

Does 1.4% tell us how many people were affected?

The total Console population is undisclosed in the cited notice. An absolute count cannot be calculated from that statement alone.

Has OpenCode published the root cause or completed fix?

The reviewed notice says the incident is ongoing and additional details cannot yet be shared. It states that the team is working with three providers to remediate. It does not establish completion.

Will an AI understanding check secure my provider credentials?

A tool such as Sphinx asks a different question: whether you can explain a committed change. Its own documentation exposes reviewer limitations and data flow. Credential storage needs its own reviewed controls.

Sources

  • Latest edited OpenCode notice
  • OpenCode product
  • Console provider gateway
  • Optional Console models
  • Distillation background
  • Sphinx documentation
  • Pele
  • Pele security
  • Pele maintainer explanation
