articles.title: Handling React.lazy Chunk Load Errors After Deployment
articles.description: Why old browser tabs request missing chunks—and how react-lazy-chunk-recover handles the failure...
articles.body_html:
Why old browser tabs request missing chunks—and how react-lazy-chunk-recover handles the failure without a reload loop.

A user leaves a React app open during a deployment. Hours later, they visit a lazy-loaded route for the first time. Their old tab requests a chunk the new deployment no longer serves. The route fails, even though it works in a fresh tab.

For example, the old tab might request Reports.a1b2.js after the server has switched to Reports.c3d4.js. The hashes are illustrative; the missing-file failure is the point. Vite documents this deployment failure mode.

I built and published react-lazy-chunk-recover to handle this case inside a React.lazy component loader. It recognizes likely chunk-load errors, allows one guarded reload, and passes a repeat failure to your Error Boundary. The package includes TypeScript declarations, lists React as a peer dependency, and has no direct runtime dependencies.

Why the usual React.lazy setup cannot recover on its own

React.lazy waits until the first render to call your loader. While the import is pending, <Suspense> shows a fallback. If the import rejects, React sends the error to the nearest Error Boundary. React also caches the loader promise and its result, so another render of the same lazy component does not simply start a new import. React describes each behavior in its lazy reference.

An Error Boundary can explain the failure. It cannot, by itself, update the old tab's asset references. A reload may do that by fetching the current HTML and application bundle—but only if your deployment serves them correctly. An unconditional reload can trap the user when the error persists.

The recovery code therefore needs two decisions: Is this likely a chunk-load error? And has this tab already tried to recover?

How react-lazy-chunk-recover works

The package recognises dynamic-import messages such as Failed to fetch dynamically imported module and ChunkLoadError. For a matching failure, it reads a sessionStorage guard. If no guard exists, it writes one and calls window.location.reload(). If a guard already exists, it throws the error to React. A successful load clears the guard, so a later deployment can get its own recovery attempt.

If the browser blocks sessionStorage, the package throws the error instead of starting a reload it cannot limit. During server-side rendering, it skips browser storage and page reloads; it rethrows the original import error.

Let's use it on a lazy route

Install the package:

npm install react-lazy-chunk-recover

Then replace the React.lazy call. Keep the lazy component at module scope, as React recommends:

import { Suspense } from 'react';
import { lazyWithRetry } from 'react-lazy-chunk-recover';

const Reports = lazyWithRetry(() => import('./Reports'), {
  moduleKey: 'reports',
});

export function ReportsRoute() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading reports…</p>}>
      <Reports />
    </Suspense>
  );
}

moduleKey gives this lazy loader its own guard. Use a stable, unique value for each logical lazy-loaded component—for example, reports and settings. Keep the value the same across renders and deployments; do not generate a random key or reuse one key for unrelated components. Without moduleKey, lazy components share the default guard, and one successful load can clear another component's recovery attempt.

Keep your Error Boundary around the route. <Suspense> handles the pending import; the Error Boundary handles a non-chunk error or a failed recovery. lazyWithRetry does not export an Error Boundary or replace the one your app already uses.

This wrapper targets components loaded through React.lazy. It is not a replacement for React Router's separate route-module lazy API or for every dynamic import in an application.

Configure retries for the failure you actually see

The default retries value is 0. That is deliberate: a second request for a deleted hashed file usually gets the same 404.

If your telemetry also shows brief network interruptions, allow a small number of in-place retries:

const Reports = lazyWithRetry(() => import('./Reports'), {
  moduleKey: 'reports',
  retries: 2,
  retryDelayMs: 250,
});

The loader makes up to two extra attempts, with the wait doubling after each attempt. It only enters the reload path if a recognised failure remains. Start with the default; add retries when your production errors justify the extra delay.

For an application that publishes a trusted, current asset manifest, getFreshModule offers one alternate import attempt before the reload. Your application must supply the URL and verify that the returned module is compatible with the running app. The package cannot derive a new hashed URL from the old import error. I would not enable that path without a defined manifest contract and a test that spans two builds.

Test it like a real deployment

Use a staging environment, not production. In this test, build A is the version already running in an open tab, and build B is the newer version on the server. Pick one lazy route, such as /reports. You want to see whether the old tab can reach the working route after its old chunk disappears.

First run: recovery succeeds

  1. Deploy build A. Open the app and leave that tab on a different route; do not open /reports yet. Check the Network panel to make sure the route's chunk has not already been prefetched.
  2. Deploy build B without refreshing the old tab. In staging, make build A's /reports chunk unavailable. If your host retains old files, block that exact old chunk URL in your browser's request-blocking tools instead.
  3. In the old tab, open /reports. The request for build A's chunk should fail. Expect one full-page reload, followed by the /reports page from build B.
  4. Use the page, not just its heading. Confirm its important backend request or action still works with build B.

Second run: recovery cannot finish

Start again with a clean browser session and repeat the setup, but make build B's /reports chunk fail too. Expect at most one automatic reload. After the second failure, your Error Boundary should appear instead of another reload.

Finally, refresh /reports directly to confirm your server serves the app on a nested URL. In automated tests, also simulate blocked sessionStorage; the package should throw the error rather than reload without a guard.

Record the chunk-load failure, the attempted reload, and whether the route works against the current backend afterwards. The reload alone does not confirm recovery.

Plan for deployment compatibility too

The wrapper handles a failure after it reaches a lazy component. Your release process also needs to decide whether an old client may keep running:

  • Retain old hashed assets only when the old client remains compatible and safe. An incompatible API change or urgent security fix may require old tabs to update instead.
  • Let browsers revalidate the HTML entry point. Vite recommends Cache-Control: no-cache for HTML in this scenario.
  • If you use Vite, review its vite:preloadError event for dynamic-import failures outside this wrapper.
  • Confirm that a full-page reload works on every client-side route.

If a release requires every open tab to update, use an explicit app-version or update policy. This package only reacts when a wrapped lazy import fails; it cannot force an update while old chunks continue to load. If the current build still cannot load the route, the package passes the failure to your Error Boundary instead of refreshing forever.

Final thoughts

A deployment can change more than file names. It can change API contracts, fix a critical bug, or remove vulnerable client code. Keeping old chunks available may avoid a 404 while leaving an old tab on a version you no longer want running.

That is why I built react-lazy-chunk-recover: when a wrapped lazy import fails, the tab gets one guarded chance to load the current build. If it still fails, your Error Boundary takes over. The package does not replace a version policy for releases that must retire every old client.

If you face stale-chunk failures, try the package on one lazy route and reproduce the two-build deployment described above. Check the route's backend interactions after the reload, not just its loading state. A reload is an attempt; a working route on the current build is recovery.

I would be interested to hear how your app handles breaking deployments and what chunk-load message your browser or bundler produces. If you try the package, share those details and whether the route worked after the reload. That feedback can help shape the next release.

ENJOY YOUR CODING! 🚀

articles.title: Sanity CMS public dataset: why my codename desk needed a review queue
articles.description: Using Sanity as a public dataset backend for a static Astro site, with a review queue for user-submitted content and a hosted Studio.
articles.body_html:
I manage codenames. Not for any organization that would pay me — just for
myself, and now for whoever else lands on the page. Cryptonym Desk started as a
private CSV that grew into something I wanted to share as a static site. The
problem was that a static site that accepts submissions isn't really static
anymore.

Here's how I rebuilt it on Astro with a public Sanity dataset, where the
review workflow lives inside Sanity itself, and where one thing I assumed
"just works" in a headless CMS almost killed the project.

The dataset as the API

The original architecture was a JSON file generated from a script, served by
Nginx. To add a codename, you edited the JSON, re-ran the build, redeployed.
Worked fine for one person. For zero other people.

Sanity's public dataset feature is what made me try it. You configure a dataset
as public, and any content published to it is readable from the CDN without
authentication. No API gateway, no token rotation, no JWT in a client that
doesn't have users. The client queries it with GROQ, same as any authenticated
Sanity project, but without a token header.

That means a static site generator like Astro can pull all published content at
build time, render pages, and ship zero JavaScript for data fetching — the
pages are just HTML. It's a headless CMS that's also your data lake, your cache
layer, and your read API, all on someone else's CDN.

It also means anyone with the project ID can query your entire published
dataset. That's the trade-off: you get a free global CDN-backed API, and you
give up any notion of private published content. For a public reference site,
that's fine. For something with user accounts, it wouldn't be.

The review gap

The problem showed up the first time someone wanted to submit a codename.

A static site has no form handler. You can put a form on the page and point it
at a serverless function or a third-party service, but then you have to wire
that response into your CMS. The straight path is a webhook that writes to
Sanity, but unauthenticated webhooks that create documents are a production
incident waiting to happen — and a spam pipeline.

What I wanted was: someone submits a word, it lands in a "pending" state
visible only to me, I approve or reject it, and if approved it appears on the
next build.

Sanity has draft and published states per document. That's nearly the workflow,
but drafts are visible to anyone with dataset write access, and a submission
that creates a draft still needs the submitter to have a token. So the pipeline
was: external form -> serverless function -> Sanity mutation with a
write-restricted token -> document in "pending" status.

That's where the queue came in. Instead of trying to make Sanity's document
workflow handle submission review, I kept submissions as a separate document
type, "wordProposal", and built a minimal review interface in a Sanity Studio
dashboard. The App SDK lets you register tools that run inside Studio — I used
it to add a queue view that lists proposals, shows the proposed word and a
submission reason if provided, and lets the editor promote it to a published
codename document or delete it.

What broke

Three things, and two of them I should have caught earlier.

First, the App SDK queue widget and mobile. The dashboard component was a
custom React widget that queried *[_type == "wordProposal"] and rendered a
list with approve/reject buttons. It worked great in the desktop Studio. On
mobile, Sanity's Studio iframe clipped the widget to a narrow column and the
buttons overflowed without scroll. The fix was wrapping the widget in a
responsive container and testing at 360px viewport width before every deploy.
I'd skipped that because "I'll only review from my laptop."

Second, the pinned appId. When you register an App SDK tool, Sanity gives
you an appId. If you don't pin the deployed version in your manifest, Studio
loads whatever you last pushed — which could be a broken build you thought was
just a test. Pinning is one checkbox in the Sanity console, but I missed it
for two weeks and once reviewed proposals against a widget that was querying
the wrong dataset because I'd deployed a dev branch.

Third, Studio as the editorial interface is fine for editors, but it's not a
public submission portal. I spent a week trying to configure the Studio
itself as a submission form — public users landing on a Studio page, filling a
custom input, hitting submit. That doesn't work because Studio requires
authentication. The boundary is clear now: Studio is for people who manage
content. The public form lives on the Astro site. The queue sits between them.

The shape of it now

The final architecture is boring in the best way:

  • Astro builds the static pages at deploy time, querying the public Sanity dataset for published codenames.
  • Sanity stores both published codenames and pending proposals as separate document types.
  • The form is an Astro page with a POST handler pointing to a lightweight serverless function that creates a proposal document with a write-restricted Sanity token.
  • The review queue is an App SDK widget registered in the Sanity Studio — a simple list with approve/reject buttons that either creates a published codename from the proposal or deletes it.
  • The hosted Studio is the deployed Studio app linked from the Astro site's admin route, so I can open it from anywhere.

The queue is data — a document type and an App SDK widget. No separate queue
service, no message broker, no database. The dataset is the source of truth for
everything, including workflow state.

The whole thing lives at
https://github.com/casareanderson/cryptonym-desk-sanity.
The documentation includes screenshots of the live desk and the corpus page,
and the Studio setup is documented step-by-step because I will forget how I
configured the App SDK tool.

The lesson that transfers

If you're using a headless CMS as your public backend, the review workflow is
not a feature — it's the product. Sanity's draft/published model is designed
for editorial teams, not for public submissions. The moment you open content to
anonymous input, you need a queue between the submitter and the published
document, and that queue has to be part of your content model, not bolted onto
it as webhooks and external databases.

Keep the queue in the dataset. A proposal document type with a status field,
an App SDK widget to process it, and a static site that only reads published
state — that's three things that each do one job and don't require a fourth
thing to coordinate them.

Don't try to make Studio a submission form. It's an editorial tool. Build your
public form separately, and don't assume the mobile layout of a custom Studio
widget works until you've looked at it from a phone.

— The public dataset is the simplest interface. The queue is the one that needs designing.

🤖 Drafted with AI assistance from my own homelab notes, logs and repos, then reviewed and edited before publishing.

articles.title: How Was State Managed in Frontend Development in the Old Days and Its Evolution?
articles.description: How frontend state was managed with vanilla JS, jQuery, and early MVC frameworks, why keeping data and the DOM in sync got painful, and what React changed.
articles.body_html:
Open a jQuery codebase from 2012 and try to answer one question: where is the cart count stored?

Maybe it's a JavaScript variable. Maybe it's the text inside <span class="cart-badge">. Maybe it's a data-count attribute on a button. Often, it's all three, and they disagree.

That disagreement is the problem React, Redux, and every state library after them were built to solve. Here is how it looked before them.

The simplest case: a counter

Plain JavaScript:

<h2 id="count">0</h2>
<button id="increment">Increment</button>

<script>
  let count = 0;

  document.getElementById("increment").addEventListener("click", () => {
    count++;
    document.getElementById("count").textContent = count;
  });
</script>

jQuery (2006 onward):

<h2 id="count">0</h2>
<button id="increment">Increment</button>

<script>
  let count = 0;

  $("#increment").on("click", function () {
    count++;
    $("#count").text(count);
  });
</script>

React:

import { useState } from "react";

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  return (
    <>
      <h2>{count}</h2>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>Increment</button>
    </>
  );
}

jQuery made selecting elements and wiring events much nicer, but look at what it did not change: you still update the variable and you still tell the DOM what to do. Two steps, both manual.

React removes the second step. You change the state, and React works out the DOM changes.

The difference is imperative (do these DOM operations) versus declarative (here is what the UI looks like for this state).

Where it breaks: the cart

A counter has one number and one place that shows it. Real apps don't.

Think of a shop with a navbar badge, a product page, a cart page, and a checkout summary. Adding an item has to update all of them:

let cart = [];

function addToCart(product) {
  cart.push(product);

  $(".cart-badge").text(cart.length);
  $("#cart-total").text(calculateTotal(cart));
  $("#product-" + product.id + " .add-btn").text("In cart");

  if (cart.length === 1) {
    $("#empty-cart-message").hide();
  }
  // ...and the checkout summary? And the "remove" flow?
}

This is an illustrative example, not code from a specific project, but the shape is very familiar. Every feature that touches the cart needs to remember every place the cart is displayed. Miss one and the UI quietly lies to the user.

Two common failure modes:

  • Forgotten update: You add a "remove" button and forget to refresh the badge.
  • DOM as the database: Someone reads parseInt($(".cart-badge").text()) because it was convenient. Now the display is the source of truth, and formatting changes like "1 item" can break logic. 
flowchart TD
    A[User clicks Add to cart] --> B[Update cart variable]
    B --> C[Update navbar badge]
    B --> D[Update product button]
    B --> E[Update cart total]
    B --> F[Update checkout summary]
    F -. forgot this one .-> G[UI out of sync]

How the tools evolved

The eras overlap, and none of them fully disappeared, but roughly:

Era Approach What it helped with What was still manual
Static HTML (1990s) Reload the page from the server Nothing to sync Any interactivity
Vanilla JS (late 1990s to 2000s) Variables + DOM APIs Dynamic pages Selecting and updating everything
jQuery (2006) Selectors, events, simpler DOM Cross-browser pain, less code State-to-DOM sync
Backbone / AngularJS (about 2010) Models, views, bindings Structure, some automatic syncing Complexity, tricky data flow
React (2013) Components render from state DOM updates Sharing state across components
Redux, MobX, Context, Zustand (2015 onward) Centralized or specialized stores Shared state at scale Choosing the right tool

Backbone gave you models that fire change events, but you still wrote the render logic. AngularJS added two-way binding, which was convenient and also made it harder to see which change caused which update.

Then React's pitch was simple: stop writing the update step. Describe the UI as a function of state.

The same cart, declaratively 

function Navbar({ cart }) {
  return <span className="cart-badge">{cart.length}</span>;
}

function CartSummary({ cart }) {
  const total = cart.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, 0);
  return <p>Total: {total}</p>;
}

function App() {
  const [cart, setCart] = useState([]);

  const addToCart = (product) => setCart((prev) => [...prev, product]);

  return (
    <>
      <Navbar cart={cart} />
      <ProductList onAdd={addToCart} />
      <CartSummary cart={cart} />
    </>
  );
}

There is no "update the badge" code. The badge is cart.length, always.

That solves rendering. It doesn't solve sharing: once many distant components need cart, passing props through layers gets awkward. That is the gap Redux filled in 2015 with a single store and explicit updates:

// Redux Toolkit
const cartSlice = createSlice({
  name: "cart",
  initialState: [],
  reducers: {
    added: (state, action) => {
      state.push(action.payload);
    },
  },
});

Whether you need Redux, Context, or Zustand is a separate question. Plenty of apps are fine with plain React state.

What to take from this

  • Old-style bugs came from duplicated state: a variable, the DOM, and sometimes an attribute, all claiming to be the truth.
  • React's biggest change was not "components." It was one source of truth that the UI is derived from.
  • State management libraries solve sharing and coordinating state, not the basic rendering problem.
  • You can still see this today: any time you read data back out of the DOM in React (ref.current.value everywhere, document.querySelector), you are partly back in the old model.

If an interviewer asks

Before React, state lived in JavaScript variables, globals, browser storage, and often the DOM itself. jQuery simplified DOM updates, and MVC frameworks like Backbone and AngularJS added structure and bindings. As apps grew, keeping data and UI consistent got hard. React introduced a declarative, component-based model where UI is derived from state, and libraries like Redux later made shared state more predictable.

And one distinction worth making: state existed long before React. React changed how state connects to the UI.

Your turn

If you worked in the jQuery or Backbone days, what was the worst "UI out of sync" bug you remember? And if you started with React, have you ever caught yourself reading values back from the DOM instead of state?

articles.title: Why CAGR Is Not the Same as Your Actual Year-by-Year Return
articles.description: CAGR is useful because it compresses a beginning value, ending value, and time span into one...
articles.body_html:
CAGR is useful because it compresses a beginning value, ending value, and time span into one annualized rate. It is also easy to misuse as if an investment grew at that rate every year. I built the calculator to show both the compact percentage and a reconstructed year-by-year path, making that distinction hard to miss.

The core formula describes an equivalent rate

The computed result normalizes the inputs and clamps the number of years:

const b = Number(beginValue.value) || 0;
const e = Number(endValue.value) || 0;
const Y = Math.min(
  Math.max(Math.floor(Number(years.value) || 0), 1),
  80
);
if (b <= 0 || e <= 0) return null;

const cagr = Math.pow(e / b, 1 / Y) - 1;

The formula asks: “What constant annual rate would turn the beginning value into the ending value over Y years?” It does not inspect the path between those endpoints. A portfolio could crash and recover and still have the same CAGR as a smooth line.

Total return answers a different question

The source keeps simple growth separate:

const totalReturn = e / b - 1;
const gain = e - b;

totalReturn is the complete change across the period. cagr is that change annualized with compounding. A 21 percent total return over three years is not a 21 percent annual return; the equivalent annual rate is smaller. Showing both prevents a familiar percentage from being read with the wrong time unit.

The yearly table is a reconstructed path

Once CAGR is known, the tool builds illustrative values:

const rows = [];
for (let y = 0; y <= Y; y++) {
  const value = b * Math.pow(1 + cagr, y);
  rows.push({
    year: y,
    value,
    growth: value - b,
  });
}

This table is not historical data. It is the smooth path implied by the equivalent rate. That makes it useful for explaining compounding, but it should not be mistaken for the actual annual returns that produced the endpoint.

The formatter makes the sign explicit:

function fmtPct(val) {
  if (val === null || val === undefined || isNaN(val)) return "—";
  const pct = val * 100;
  const sign = pct > 0 ? "+" : "";
  return `${sign}${pct.toFixed(2)}%`;
}

Negative CAGR is valid when the ending value is lower, while zero gets no plus sign. The input guard rejects zero or negative endpoints because the logarithmic intuition behind growth rates becomes misleading for this simple ratio model.

The major limitation is what the formula leaves out: deposits, withdrawals, dividends, taxes, fees, inflation, volatility, and cash-flow timing. If money enters or leaves during the period, a money-weighted or time-weighted return measure may be more appropriate. The 80-year cap is also a display boundary, not a statement about finance.

A smooth chart can be honest if it labels the assumption

The reconstructed rows start at year zero, where value equals the beginning value and growth is zero. Each later row compounds the same equivalent rate again. That makes the table a teaching aid: it shows what “annualized” means without claiming that the account actually followed that line.

There is also a useful relationship to check manually. The final row should equal the ending input apart from floating-point and display rounding, because the rate was derived from that endpoint. gain should equal end - begin, while the cumulative growth in the last row should express the same difference. These simple invariants are valuable when changing a financial component; they catch swapped endpoints and off-by-one year loops quickly.

Negative results deserve the same care as positive ones. If the ending value is lower, fmtPct adds no plus sign and the reconstructed path declines each year. That path is still only an equivalent path. A real investment can have negative years followed by recovery, and CAGR alone cannot tell the story of volatility or drawdown.

If a future version adds cash flows, I would not quietly overload these inputs. I would introduce a separate return method and explain its assumptions, because a single “CAGR” label should not start pretending to be an internal rate of return calculator.

The formatter rounds currency-like values to whole units while leaving the percentage at two decimal places. That is a display choice, not a loss of precision in the calculation. Keeping raw numeric fields in the returned result means another presentation—more decimals, a chart tooltip, or a localized currency symbol—can be added without rewriting the formula.

That split between raw result and formatted text is especially helpful when comparing two scenarios: the UI can show friendly numbers while tests still inspect the unrounded cagr, gain, and row values.

The final result remains a model, not a guarantee, and the input values still need context before anyone makes a decision.

I would also avoid comparing CAGR values with different time windows as if they were automatically equivalent. The exponent normalizes each result to an annual rate, but a two-year result and a twenty-year result can have very different uncertainty, volatility, and practical meaning. The component can calculate both because the formula is compact; interpretation still belongs to the person supplying the beginning and ending values.

That boundary is useful for implementation too. The view does not fetch market prices, infer missing dates, or decorate the result with a prediction. It receives three numbers, calculates a reproducible equivalent rate, and exposes the intermediate rows. Fewer hidden inputs make the output easier to audit, even when the financial story behind those inputs is complicated.

I turned this explanation into a small free tool: CAGR Calculator.
